title: Bootes: Boosting the Efficiency of Sparse Accelerators Using Spectral Clustering
problem: Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (SpGEMM) accelerators using row-wise product dataflow suffer from poor off-chip memory traffic because row reordering — the primary technique to improve data reuse — is either suboptimal, slow to compute, or fails to detect when reordering is counterproductive for certain sparsity patterns.
method: Bootes applies spectral clustering to reorder rows of the input matrix A before feeding them into a row-wise SpGEMM accelerator. A similarity matrix capturing structural properties of A's row sparsity patterns guides the clustering; similar rows are placed adjacent so that their accesses into B have high overlap, maximizing data reuse. The spectral clustering algorithm itself is optimized to reduce preprocessing time to a geometric mean of 11.61x faster than existing reordering techniques. A decision tree model trained on real-world sparse matrices predicts whether reordering will be beneficial before executing it, enabling cost-aware preprocessing that avoids overhead when reordering would increase traffic.

title: HiPER: Hierarchically-Composed Processing for Efficient Robot Learning-Based Control
problem: Learning-Based Model Predictive Control (LMPC) for robot navigation combines neural network inference with iterative MPC optimization, creating a mixed workload with rapidly varying computational patterns that neither GPUs nor simple CPU-GPU integrations can serve efficiently. The workload alternates between dense ML computation and sparse, irregular MPC solves across time steps.
method: HiPER is a 1024-PE ASIC synthesized in 16nm CMOS (16.37 mm²) built around a fractal interconnect topology that nests local systolic arrays within a hierarchical extension to handle the traffic characteristics of LMPC. A six-level pointer queue hierarchy orchestrates program composition and execution, enabling temporal and spatial mapping of workload phases at runtime. The pointer queues serve as a lightweight control mechanism that composes heterogeneous sub-programs without a complex scheduler, allowing dynamic adaptation to workload changes.

title: NVMePass: A Lightweight, High-performance and Scalable NVMe Virtualization Architecture with I/O Queues Passthrough
problem: Existing NVMe virtualization approaches either suffer severe performance degradation (Virtio software path) or require dedicated hardware with limited VM scalability (VFIO/SR-IOV hardware passthrough). No solution simultaneously achieves near-native I/O performance, zero CPU overhead, and high VM count scalability.
method: NVMePass is a software-hardware co-design that passes NVMe I/O queues directly to VMs, enabling VMs to submit commands and receive completions without hypervisor involvement. DMA and interrupt remapping are handled without hypervisor interposition. A new hardware primitive, the NVMe Resource Domain (NRD), is implemented in the NVMe controller to enforce VM-level isolation by intercepting illegal I/O requests. Logical block address ranges and I/O queues are exclusively allocated per VM for isolation without per-operation hypervisor overhead.

title: ShadowBinding: Realizing Effective Microarchitectures for In-Core Secure Speculation Schemes
problem: Secure speculation schemes that mitigate Spectre-class speculative side-channel attacks (such as STT and NDA) lack rigorous RTL-level microarchitectural implementations and realistic performance/cost analysis, causing prior work to significantly underestimate their overhead. Specifically, STT's rename-stage taint computation creates an expensive single-cycle dependency chain that degrades performance on wider out-of-order cores.
method: ShadowBinding develops concrete RTL microarchitectures for two state-of-the-art secure speculation schemes—Speculative Taint Tracking (STT) and Non-Speculative Data Access (NDA)—implemented on the RISC-V Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). For STT, a novel variant called STT-Issue is proposed that delays taint computation from the rename stage to the issue stage, breaking the expensive single-cycle rename-stage dependency chain and improving IPC, area, and timing. RTL synthesis and cycle-accurate simulation are used to measure the combined IPC and timing impact, capturing the full performance loss including clock frequency degradation.

title: Gigaflow: Pipeline-Aware Sub-Traversal Caching for Modern SmartNICs
problem: Virtual switch (vSwitch) offloading to SmartNICs suffers from high cache miss rates and poor scalability as the flow rule space grows, because existing solutions cannot efficiently store or traverse the large and complex flow rule tables that modern cloud tenants require. This leads to bottlenecks in packet processing throughput at the NIC level.
method: Gigaflow introduces pipeline-aware sub-traversal caching, which decomposes multi-stage vSwitch packet processing pipelines into sub-traversals and caches intermediate traversal results rather than only caching complete flow lookups. By being aware of the pipeline structure, Gigaflow identifies which sub-traversal results can be safely reused across multiple packets, reducing redundant flow rule table traversals and improving NIC cache hit rates even for large flow rule spaces.

title: Faster Chaitin-like Register Allocation via Grammatical Decompositions of Control-Flow Graphs
problem: Register allocation via graph coloring (Chaitin-style) is NP-hard in general, but practical compilers rely on heuristics that do not exploit the sparse, structured nature of real program control-flow graphs (CFGs). This leads to suboptimal allocation or unnecessary spills in programs with structured control flow.
method: The paper formalizes the sparsity of structured program CFGs using graph-theoretic parameters (treewidth, pathwidth) and introduces a grammatical decomposition—parsing the CFG into a tree decomposition. Register allocation is then solved efficiently via dynamic programming on this tree decomposition, yielding a parameterized algorithm whose complexity scales with the treewidth of the CFG rather than graph size alone. This exploits the observation that real programs' CFGs have small treewidth, making previously intractable exact or near-exact coloring feasible.

title: Fast On-device LLM Inference with NPUs
problem: On-device LLM inference on mobile NPUs incurs unacceptably high latency, particularly during the prefill stage, because existing NPU programming models are not designed to efficiently map the irregular, attention-heavy computation patterns of LLMs. Even mobile-sized models (e.g., Gemma-2B) run too slowly for interactive tasks such as screen UI understanding.
method: The system analyzes the NPU execution bottlenecks of mobile LLMs and redesigns the inference pipeline to exploit NPU-specific parallelism. It introduces operator fusion and tiling strategies tailored to NPU dataflow constraints, and reorders computation to overlap NPU and CPU execution. The approach targets the prefill stage specifically, batching token processing to amortize NPU invocation overhead and restructuring attention kernels to fit the NPU's fixed-function units.

title: Adaptive CHERI Compartmentalization for Heterogeneous Accelerators
problem: Hardware accelerators in heterogeneous systems lack fine-grained memory protection: IOMMU-based isolation operates at page granularity, leaving intra-page accesses unprotected, while per-accelerator memory safety modifications require significant engineering effort and do not scale across diverse accelerator types.
method: CapChecker is an adaptive hardware interface inserted between CHERI-unaware accelerators and the system memory bus. It imports capability metadata from the CPU's CHERI register file and enforces pointer-level bounds and permission checks on every memory access issued by the accelerator, without modifying the accelerator architecture itself. The interface interposes on the accelerator's memory request channel, decodes the capability tag and bounds from the CPU-managed capability table, and raises a fault on any out-of-bounds or permission-violating access. Capability grants from the CPU are communicated through a lightweight descriptor mechanism that maps accelerator DMA addresses to CHERI capabilities.

title: Drishti: Do Not Forget Slicing While Designing Last-Level Cache Replacement Policies for Many-Core Systems
problem: State-of-the-art LLC replacement policies (Hawkeye, Mockingjay) use a per-slice sampled cache and a per-slice reuse predictor that make myopic decisions based only on accesses to a single slice, unaware of global reuse behavior across all LLC slices in many-core systems; additionally, per-slice sampled cache sets receive insufficient LLC misses to drive accurate replacement decisions.
method: Drishti proposes two enhancements to existing LLC replacement policies for sliced LLCs: (1) a per-core global reuse predictor where each core's predictor is trained on all accesses by that core across all LLC slices—achieving global reuse awareness without centralized inter-slice interconnect traffic—combined with a local (per-slice) sampled cache that remains slice-local; (2) a per-slice dynamic sampled cache that adaptively expands the set of LLC sets used for sampling to improve the sample quality and ensure adequate miss coverage per slice. Evaluated by augmenting Hawkeye and Mockingjay on 4, 16, and 32-core systems with 8, 32, and 64 MB sliced LLCs.

title: Towards End-to-End Optimization of LLM-based Applications with Ayo
problem: LLM-based applications consist of both LLM and non-LLM components whose combined end-to-end latency is not jointly optimized by existing frameworks, which use coarse-grained task-module orchestration that confines optimizations within individual modules.
method: Ayo introduces a fine-grained, end-to-end workflow optimizer for LLM-based applications that breaks down application pipelines below the task-module boundary, enabling cross-module scheduling decisions. The system models the full application DAG and applies joint optimization of LLM inference scheduling alongside non-LLM compute stages to minimize overall pipeline latency.

title: CROSS: Compiler-Driven Optimization of Sparse DNNs Using Sparse/Dense Computation Kernels
problem: Exploiting DNN weight sparsity on GPUs is hindered by the overhead of index-based encoding/decoding required by sparse formats, making sparse computation kernels slower than dense kernels even at high sparsity ratios.
method: CROSS is an end-to-end compilation framework that analyzes parameter distribution locality to identify regions where dense computation remains efficient. It decomposes sparse DNN workloads into multiple components across different sparsity levels and maps each component to either a specialized sparse kernel or a high-performance dense kernel. A novel sparse graph translation technique transforms the sparse computation graph into a form compatible with dense computation kernels, reconciling the sparse DNN computation with optimized BLAS-level dense routines on GPU. The framework accommodates various sparsity patterns (unstructured, structured, N:M) and optimization techniques.

title: Earth+: On-Board Satellite Imagery Compression Leveraging Historical Earth Observations
problem: Satellite downlink capacity is so limited that over 90% of captured earth-observation images are never downloaded; existing on-board compression techniques treat each image independently and cannot exploit the rich temporal and spatial redundancy available across an entire satellite constellation.
method: Earth+ implements a change-detection-based compression pipeline on the satellite. Ground stations upload recently captured reference images from other satellites in the same constellation to each on-board satellite via the uplink. On-board processing compares each newly captured image against the latest matching reference image and transmits only the changed regions (delta encoding). The system manages reference image currency and on-board storage to ensure that references are temporally close to the captured images, maximizing delta sparsity and thus compression.

title: BrokenSleep: Remote Power Timing Attack Exploiting Processor Idle States
problem: Modern processors support multiple C-state (idle) levels with different wake-up latencies; an attacker can remotely detect which C-state a victim processor core is in by measuring network response timing, enabling covert and side-channel communication across nodes without requiring co-location on the same machine.
method: BrokenSleep exploits the deterministic wake-up latency differences between processor C-states (C0 active, C1/C1E/C6 sleep) to encode information in the timing of network responses from a victim server. The attacker sends network requests and measures response latency; the victim's current C-state (determined by its workload idle pattern) is deduced from the latency profile. Both covert channel (data exfiltration across security boundaries without direct network access) and side-channel (keystroke timing inference) variants are demonstrated. The attack affects both Intel and ARM processors, exploiting standard ACPI power management without any microarchitectural vulnerability.

title: WarpDrive: GPU-Based Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration Leveraging Tensor and CUDA Cores
problem: GPU-based acceleration of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is bottlenecked by frequent pipeline stalls from memory-latency-bound Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) operations and by suboptimal utilization of GPU hardware units, leaving both CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores underused for FHE workloads.
method: WarpDrive applies three key optimizations: (1) computation decomposition of NTT that reduces total instruction count by 73% through arithmetic restructuring; (2) fine-grained memory access design that pipelines loads to eliminate 86% of pipeline stalls; (3) a concurrent-execution framework that runs CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores simultaneously within a single NTT kernel — the first such combined use — exploiting both unit types' complementary throughput characteristics. Additionally, intra-ciphertext parallelism is maximally extracted without requiring ciphertext batching.

title: GoPIM: GCN-Oriented Pipeline Optimization for PIM Accelerators
problem: ReRAM-based PIM accelerators for GCN training suffer from severe pipeline underutilization due to skewed execution times across GCN stages (aggregation, combination) and skewed degree distributions of graph vertices, causing crossbar resource imbalance.
method: GoPIM employs an ML-based scheme that dynamically allocates ReRAM crossbar resources to the most needed pipeline stages to streamline overall execution and eliminate stage bottlenecks. A selective vertex updating technique interleaves vertex mapping across crossbars to evenly distribute vertices despite skewed degree distributions. These two mechanisms reduce overall execution time while maintaining accuracy. A practical architecture design for GoPIM is also provided.

title: Performance Prediction of On-NIC Network Functions with Multi-Resource Contention and Traffic Awareness
problem: Co-located network functions (NFs) on SmartNICs suffer performance interference from multi-resource contention (CPU cores, memory bandwidth, DMA engines, queues), but existing performance prediction models lack SmartNIC-specific knowledge and traffic-pattern awareness, yielding poor prediction accuracy for SLA management. Operators cannot efficiently allocate SmartNIC resources without accurate contention-aware performance predictions.
method: The paper develops a performance prediction framework that models SmartNIC-specific resource contention by profiling the interactions between co-located NFs across multiple resource dimensions (CPU, memory, interconnects). The model incorporates traffic awareness by accounting for how arrival patterns and traffic rates influence queuing delays and per-NF throughput under contention. Machine learning or analytical models (details from abstract) are used to predict NF latency and throughput given a resource allocation and traffic profile.
